30 Which charge can be carried by a charge carrier?
A
1.1  10–19
C
B
4.0  10–19
C
C
4.8  10–19
C
D
9.1  10–19
C

hints: Notice the four values are all around $10^{-19} \text{ C}$, so compare each one with the elementary charge $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$.
Recall that any free charge $Q$ must satisfy $Q = ne$ where $n$ is a whole number of electrons or ions.
Divide each listed charge in $\text{C}$ by $1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ and look for the one that gives an exact integer.
walkthrough: Identify the rule for this question: charge is quantised, so a charge carrier must carry $Q = ne$, where $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ and $n = 1, 2, 3...$.
Rearrange to test each option: $n = Q / e$. Only a value giving a whole number for $n$ is possible.
Check the options: for $1.1 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, $n \approx 0.69$; for $4.0 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, $n = 2.5$; for $9.1 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, $n \approx 5.69$.
For $4.8 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, $n = (4.8 \times 10^{-19}) / (1.6 \times 10^{-19}) = 3.0$, which is an exact whole number of elementary charges.
Therefore $4.8 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ can be carried as $3e$. This is option C.

A.explanation: Dividing $1.1 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ by $1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ gives about 0.69, which is not a whole number so cannot be a quantised charge.

B.explanation: Dividing $4.0 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ by $1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ gives 2.5, which is not a whole number of elementary charges.

C.explanation: Dividing $4.8 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ by $1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ gives exactly 3, so it equals $3e$ and is allowed.

D.explanation: Dividing $9.1 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ by $1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ gives about 5.7, which is not a whole number so cannot be a single carrier charge.
